terms.def: The part of a station that turns the transmitter's electrical power into radio waves, and turns arriving radio waves back into electrical signals.
terms.more: An antenna cannot add power. It can only send the power it is given more strongly in some directions than in others.

terms.def: An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction.
terms.more: A Yagi is a common beam antenna. Concentrating the signal one way is what gives a beam its gain.

terms.def: A beam antenna with several parallel elements that focus the signal in one direction.
terms.more: Of the 5/8 wave vertical, isotropic, J pole and Yagi, the Yagi offers the greatest gain.

terms.def: The increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared to a reference antenna.
terms.more: Gain is not added power: the antenna sends more signal one way and less another. A Yagi has high gain, and a 5/8-wavelength whip has more gain than a 1/4-wave antenna.

terms.def: A simple standard antenna that other antennas are compared with when stating their gain.
terms.more: Common references are a dipole and an isotropic antenna, a theoretical point that radiates equally in every direction.

terms.def: Making a physically short antenna act electrically longer.
terms.more: One type of loading is inserting inductors (coils) in the radiating elements. A longer electrical length means a lower resonant frequency.

terms.def: A coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field.
terms.more: Inserting inductors in an antenna's radiating elements electrically lengthens the antenna. This is a type of antenna loading.

terms.def: The part of an antenna, usually a wire, rod or tube, that sends out and picks up radio waves.
terms.more: Inductors can be inserted in radiating elements to make a short antenna electrically longer.

terms.def: The direction in which the electric field of an antenna's radio wave points, such as vertical or horizontal.
terms.more: It is described by the orientation of the electric field, not the magnetic field. An upright element gives vertical polarization.

terms.def: One of the two fields that make up a radio wave; the other is the magnetic field, at right angles to it.
terms.more: The orientation of the electric field is what describes an antenna's polarization.

terms.def: The short flexible antenna supplied with a handheld radio.
terms.more: Compared with a full-sized quarter-wave antenna its disadvantage is low efficiency.

terms.def: How much of the power fed to an antenna is actually radiated as radio waves instead of being lost.
terms.more: A handheld radio's short flexible antenna has low efficiency compared with a full-sized quarter-wave antenna.

terms.def: A small portable radio that transmits and receives and is held in the hand.
terms.more: Its short flexible antenna has low efficiency. Used inside a vehicle without an external antenna, its signal strength is reduced by the shielding effect of the vehicle.

terms.def: The blocking of radio signals by metal that surrounds the antenna.
terms.more: A vehicle's body shields a handheld used inside it, so signal strength is reduced. An externally mounted antenna avoids this.

terms.def: An antenna whose radiating element is about one quarter of a wavelength long.
terms.more: On 2 meters a resonant quarter-wave vertical is about 19 inches long. A 5/8-wavelength whip has more gain than a 1/4-wave antenna.

terms.def: An antenna with a single upright radiating element.
terms.more: A 19-inch vertical is often used on 2 meters because it is a resonant quarter-wave.

terms.def: A vertical antenna whose element is five eighths of a wavelength long.
terms.more: For VHF or UHF mobile service its advantage over a 1/4-wave antenna is that it has more gain.

terms.def: A thin, flexible rod antenna, commonly mounted on vehicles.
terms.more: A 5/8-wavelength whip has more gain than a 1/4-wave antenna for VHF or UHF mobile service.

terms.def: Operating a radio from a vehicle.
terms.more: Mobile stations use an antenna mounted outside the vehicle, because the vehicle's body shields an antenna inside it and reduces signal strength.

terms.def: The frequency at which an antenna's length suits the wavelength, so the antenna works naturally there.
terms.more: Shortening a dipole increases its resonant frequency. A 19-inch vertical is a resonant quarter-wave on 2 meters.

terms.def: A simple antenna made of a straight wire or rod, usually half a wavelength long, fed at its center.
terms.more: A half-wave dipole radiates the strongest signal broadside to the antenna. Shortening a dipole increases its resonant frequency.

terms.def: At right angles to the length of an antenna wire.
terms.more: A half-wave dipole radiates its strongest signal broadside to the antenna, and least off its ends.

terms.def: A description of how strongly an antenna radiates in each direction.
terms.more: A half-wave dipole's pattern is strongest broadside to the antenna. A beam antenna's pattern is concentrated in one direction.

terms.def: The distance a radio wave travels during one complete cycle.
terms.more: Antenna lengths are given as fractions of a wavelength, such as quarter-wave, half-wave and 5/8-wave. A quarter wavelength on 2 meters is about 19 inches.

terms.def: The amateur VHF band with a wavelength of about 2 meters.
terms.more: A 19-inch vertical antenna is often used on this band because it is a resonant quarter-wave.

terms.def: The cable that carries radio signals between the radio and the antenna.
terms.more: Coaxial cable is the most common type. Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss. A loose connection in the feed line can cause erratic changes in SWR.

terms.def: A feed line with a center wire surrounded by insulation and an outer metal shield.
terms.more: It is the most common feed line because it is easy to use and needs few special installation considerations. The most common impedance is 50 ohms. Loss increases as frequency increases.

terms.def: The opposition a circuit, cable or antenna presents to alternating current, measured in ohms.
terms.more: The most common impedance of coaxial cable in amateur radio is 50 ohms. An antenna tuner matches the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance.

terms.def: The unit used to measure resistance and impedance.
terms.more: The most common coaxial cable used in amateur radio has an impedance of 50 ohms.

terms.def: A device placed between the radio and the antenna system that changes the impedance the radio sees.
terms.more: Its major function is to match the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance.

terms.def: Making the impedance of one part of the antenna system equal to that of the part it connects to, so power passes between them without being reflected.
terms.more: SWR measures how well a load is matched to a transmission line. An antenna tuner matches the antenna system to the transceiver.

terms.def: A radio that combines a transmitter and a receiver in one unit.
terms.more: An antenna tuner matches the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance.

terms.def: Standing wave ratio: a measure of how well a load is matched to a transmission line.
terms.more: A perfect match is 1:1. High SWR is a source of loss in coaxial feed line. Erratic changes in SWR can be caused by a loose connection in the antenna or feed line.

terms.def: Whatever is connected to the far end of a feed line and receives the power, usually the antenna.
terms.more: SWR is a measure of how well the load is matched to the transmission line.

terms.def: Signal power that is wasted, mostly as heat, inside the feed line instead of reaching the antenna or the receiver.
terms.more: Loss in coax increases with frequency. Water in connectors, high SWR and multiple connectors all add loss. RG-213 has less loss than RG-58, and air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss.

terms.def: The number of complete cycles a radio wave makes each second, measured in hertz.
terms.more: Shortening a dipole increases its resonant frequency. As the frequency of a signal in coaxial cable is increased, the loss increases.

terms.def: A plug or socket that joins a coaxial cable to a radio, an antenna or another cable.
terms.more: Common types are PL-259, BNC and Type N. Outdoors they should be carefully taped for weather protection. Multiple connectors in a line add loss.

terms.def: A threaded, screw-on coaxial cable plug.
terms.more: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies. They are not watertight and are not a bayonet type, so tape them carefully outdoors.

terms.def: A small bayonet-type coaxial cable connector that locks with a push and a twist.
terms.more: Like PL-259 and Type N connectors, it should be carefully taped for weather protection when used outdoors.

terms.def: A threaded coaxial cable connector designed to work well at UHF and higher frequencies.
terms.more: It is the connector type most suitable for frequencies above 400 MHz. It should still be carefully taped for weather protection outdoors.

terms.def: Sealing outdoor connectors, for example with tape, so that water cannot get in.
terms.more: PL-259, BNC and Type N connectors should all be carefully taped outdoors. Water intrusion into coaxial connectors is a source of feed line loss.

terms.def: A thin, flexible type of 50-ohm coaxial cable.
terms.more: It has more loss at a given frequency than the thicker RG-213.

terms.def: A thick type of 50-ohm coaxial cable.
terms.more: It has less loss at a given frequency than the thinner RG-58.

terms.def: A stiff coaxial feed line with a solid metal outer shield.
terms.more: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss of the common feed line types, lower than flexible 50-ohm or 75-ohm coax.

terms.def: High frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 3 to 30 MHz.
terms.more: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies.

terms.def: Very high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 30 MHz to 300 MHz.
terms.more: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at HF and VHF. For VHF mobile use, a 5/8-wavelength whip has more gain than a 1/4-wave antenna.

terms.def: Ultra high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 300 to 3000 MHz.
terms.more: Above 400 MHz the Type N connector is the most suitable RF connector. Coax loss is higher at UHF than at lower frequencies.
